triage.name: Renal cell carcinoma
triage.reason: Often incidental but can present with hematuria, flank mass and paraneoplastic findings; imaging-based diagnosis with a teachable differential.

risk_factors.text: Long-term dialysis or end-stage kidney disease
Occupational exposure to trichloroethylene or cadmium

family_history: Kidney cancer in a first-degree relative

chief_complaints.text: I noticed blood in my urine
I've been feeling tired and run down
I have a dull ache in my side
My doctor found something on a scan I had for another reason

hpi.onset: Often gradual and unnoticed; many tumors are found incidentally on imaging done for another reason. When symptoms occur, they usually develop over weeks to months.
hpi.duration: Weeks to months; hematuria may be intermittent
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive. Hematuria may come and go. Constitutional symptoms and flank pain tend to worsen as the tumor enlarges or invades.
hpi.location: Flank or abdominal mass; hematuria is painless and diffuse
hpi.radiation: Flank pain may radiate to the back or groin but usually does not
hpi.quality: Dull, constant flank ache; hematuria is painless and may be visible or only microscopic
hpi.severity: Variable; flank pain is usually mild to moderate, hematuria is painless
hpi.timing: Hematuria may be intermittent; flank pain is often constant

associated_symptoms.text: Dull pain in the side or back
A lump I can feel in my belly or side
Swelling in my legs or ankles
New or worsening high blood pressure

pertinent_negatives: Passing urine more often or urgently
Recent sore throat or skin infection
Colicky pain that comes in waves
Recent trauma to the flank or abdomen
Family history of bleeding or clotting disorder

argues_against: High fever with rigors suggesting pyelonephritis
Dysuria and frequency suggesting urinary tract infection
Colicky pain radiating to the groin suggesting kidney stones
Paraneoplastic syndromes such as hypercalcemia or Cushing syndrome

atypical.how_it_differs: More likely to be found incidentally on imaging and less likely to report pain or hematuria; may present with nonspecific fatigue or anemia.
Patients on dialysis or with end-stage kidney disease may have acquired cystic kidney disease and present with hematuria or an incidental mass; constitutional symptoms may be attributed to uremia.
May present with more aggressive disease and systemic symptoms, and imaging findings may be confused with infection or post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder.
Renal masses may be found incidentally on obstetric ultrasound; hematuria may be attributed to urinary tract infection or pregnancy-related changes.
missing_classic_features: Classic triad of hematuria, flank pain and mass

general.mild: Well-appearing, no distress; tumor often found incidentally
general.moderate: Mildly uncomfortable, able to lie flat for examination
general.severe: Ill-appearing, fatigued, may have visible weight loss
general.critical: Cachectic or toxic-appearing, pale, in distress from pain or hematuria

labs.caveat: Normocytic anemia from chronic disease or hematuria; a normal hemoglobin does not exclude the tumor.
Reactive thrombocytosis; also a paraneoplastic finding.
Needed before contrast imaging and to plan surgery; may be normal with a small tumor.
Paraneoplastic hypercalcemia from PTHrP or bone metastases; check ionized or corrected calcium if albumin is low.
Nonspecific; marked elevation suggests bulky or metastatic disease.
May reflect bone metastases or liver involvement.
Microscopic or gross hematuria is the most common urinary finding; a negative dipstick does not exclude the tumor.
Dysmorphic red cells and casts are absent; their presence points to glomerular disease instead.

imaging.preferred_when: First-line for a suspected renal mass in adults with adequate kidney function

Cystic or complex cystic mass with thick walls or septa (cystic renal cell carcinoma)

imaging.preferred_when: Bone pain or an elevated alkaline phosphatase

Baseline kidney function and calcium before contrast imaging and surgery
Confirms hematuria and looks for infection or glomerular disease

neurologic symptoms or known metastatic disease

No role in the evaluation of a renal mass
Not needed unless the pain is epigastric
Not part of the initial workup of an incidental small mass

bone pain or elevated alkaline phosphatase

decision_points: Pregnancy test before CT in anyone who could be pregnant
Check kidney function before iodinated contrast; use MRI or ultrasound when eGFR is low
A solid enhancing renal mass is presumed renal cell carcinoma until proven otherwise
Biopsy is not needed before resection of a clearly resectable mass
Stage with chest imaging once the diagnosis is confirmed

differential.name: Upper tract urothelial carcinoma
differential.why_considered: Painless hematuria in an older adult, often with a filling defect or mass in the collecting system
differential.trigger: Gross or microscopic hematuria with a filling defect in the renal pelvis or ureter on imaging

history: Painless gross hematuria is the dominant symptom
Occupational exposure to aromatic amines or dyes
exam: May have flank pain if the tumor obstructs the ureter
labs: Cytology may show malignant urothelial cells
imaging: Filling defect in the renal pelvis or ureter on CT urography
Soft-tissue mass centered in the collecting system rather than the renal cortex
Hydronephrosis from ureteral obstruction

differential.name: Renal oncocytoma
differential.why_considered: A solid enhancing renal mass that is benign but can look identical to renal cell carcinoma on imaging

history: No constitutional symptoms or weight loss
imaging: Homogeneous solid renal mass with a central stellate scar on CT or MRI
No venous thrombus or lymphadenopathy
Often cannot be reliably distinguished from renal cell carcinoma without biopsy or resection

differential.name: Renal angiomyolipoma
differential.why_considered: A solid renal mass that can bleed and cause flank pain or hematuria

history: History of tuberous sclerosis complex or sporadic angiomyolipoma
exam: Signs of tuberous sclerosis such as facial angiofibromas or hypopigmented macules
labs: Hematuria if the tumor bleeds into the collecting system
Falling hemoglobin if there is significant retroperitoneal hemorrhage
imaging: Macroscopic fat within the mass on CT or MRI is characteristic
Fat-poor angiomyolipoma can mimic renal cell carcinoma

differential.name: Renal abscess
differential.why_considered: Fever, flank pain and a renal mass on imaging
differential.trigger: Fever with rigors, flank pain and a cystic or complex renal lesion

history: Acute onset of fever, chills and flank pain
Recent urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis
imaging: Complex cystic or rim-enhancing fluid collection in the kidney
Perinephric fat stranding
No solid enhancing mass

differential.name: Polycystic kidney disease
differential.why_considered: Bilateral enlarged kidneys with multiple cystic lesions and hematuria

history: Family history of polycystic kidney disease
exam: Signs of chronic kidney disease such as pallor
imaging: Numerous bilateral renal cysts of varying sizes
Enlarged kidneys with preserved renal outline
No single dominant solid enhancing mass

differential.name: Renal lymphoma
differential.why_considered: A renal mass with constitutional symptoms such as fever, night sweats and weight loss

history: B symptoms: fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss
imaging: Multiple bilateral homogeneous renal masses
Retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy
Minimal enhancement compared with renal cell carcinoma

differential.name: Metastasis to the kidney
differential.why_considered: A renal mass in a patient with a known primary cancer elsewhere

history: Known primary malignancy such as lung, breast, colon or melanoma
exam: Findings related to the primary tumor
labs: Abnormal liver enzymes or tumor markers related to the primary
imaging: Multiple bilateral renal masses
Widespread metastases elsewhere
Biopsy shows histology matching the known primary

severity.mild: Small, localized tumor found incidentally; no symptoms, normal kidney function, no metastases
severity.moderate: Larger localized tumor with hematuria, flank pain or paraneoplastic findings; no distant metastases
severity.severe: Locally advanced or metastatic disease with significant symptoms, anemia, hypercalcemia or venous thrombus
severity.critical: Life-threatening complications such as massive hemorrhage, tumor thrombus extending into the inferior vena cava or right atrium, or brain metastases with raised intracranial pressure

red_flags.meaning: Massive retroperitoneal or urinary tract hemorrhage; needs urgent resuscitation and urologic intervention

red_flags.finding: New lower extremity edema, abdominal distention or dilated abdominal veins
red_flags.meaning: Inferior vena cava tumor thrombus causing venous obstruction

red_flags.finding: Severe headache, confusion, seizures or focal neurologic deficits
red_flags.meaning: Brain metastases or hypercalcemia; needs urgent imaging and management

red_flags.finding: Calcium above 12 mg/dL or symptomatic hypercalcemia
Rapidly enlarging flank mass with severe pain
red_flags.meaning: Tumor hemorrhage or rapid progression; needs urgent evaluation

complications.name: Inferior vena cava tumor thrombus
clues: Filling defect in the renal vein or IVC on CT or MRI

complications.name: Chronic kidney disease
clues: Loss of renal parenchyma after nephrectomy

special_populations.differences: More likely to be found incidentally and less likely to report pain or hematuria; may present with nonspecific fatigue, anemia or weight loss. Treatment decisions must weigh competing comorbidities and frailty.

Patients on dialysis or with end-stage kidney disease may have acquired cystic kidney disease and present with hematuria or an incidental mass. Contrast imaging requires careful planning and nephrology input.

Renal masses may be found incidentally on obstetric ultrasound; hematuria may be attributed to urinary tract infection or pregnancy-related changes. MRI without gadolinium is preferred when imaging is needed.
May present with more aggressive disease and systemic symptoms; imaging findings may be confused with infection or post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder.

cancer.screening: There is no recommended routine screening for renal cell carcinoma in the general population. Screening is not recommended by the USPSTF. Surveillance imaging may be considered in high-risk groups such as those with von Hippel-Lindau disease or other hereditary syndromes, but this is not general population screening.
cancer.pathology: Renal cell carcinoma arises from the renal tubular epithelium. The most common histologic subtype is clear cell (conventional) renal cell carcinoma, followed by papillary and chromophobe subtypes. Clear cell tumors are associated with inactivation of the von Hippel-Lindau gene and are typically hypervascular. Papillary and chromophobe subtypes have different genetic drivers and generally a better prognosis than clear cell carcinoma.
cancer.staging_concepts: Staging uses the TNM system. T stage describes the size and local extent of the tumor, including invasion of perinephric fat, renal sinus, renal vein or inferior vena cava, and extension beyond Gerota fascia or into the adrenal gland. N stage describes regional lymph node involvement. M stage describes distant metastases. Stage groups range from stage I (confined to the kidney, 7 cm or less) to stage IV (distant metastases or invasion beyond Gerota fascia). Stage is the strongest predictor of prognosis.

key_questions.question: Have you noticed blood in your urine, and if so, was it painful?
key_questions.looking_for: Painless gross or microscopic hematuria; painless bleeding in an older adult points to a renal or urothelial tumor rather than infection or stones

key_questions.question: Have you had any imaging of your abdomen or kidneys for another reason recently?
key_questions.looking_for: An incidental renal mass found on ultrasound or CT done for an unrelated complaint, which is now the most common way this tumor is found

key_questions.question: Do you have a dull ache or heaviness in your side or back?
key_questions.looking_for: Constant, non-colicky flank or back discomfort rather than the waves of renal colic

key_questions.question: Have you lost weight without trying, or had fevers, night sweats or unusual tiredness?
key_questions.looking_for: Constitutional symptoms suggesting a malignancy or paraneoplastic effect

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any new swelling in your legs, abdominal bloating, or prominent veins on your belly?
key_questions.looking_for: Signs of inferior vena cava tumor thrombus causing venous obstruction

key_questions.question: Have you had any confusion, constipation, excessive thirst or frequent urination?
Have you ever smoked cigarettes, and for how long?
key_questions.looking_for: Current or former smoking, the strongest modifiable risk factor

key_questions.question: Have you been on dialysis or been told you have kidney disease or cysts in your kidneys?
key_questions.looking_for: End-stage kidney disease with acquired cystic kidney disease, a strong risk factor

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had kidney cancer or a hereditary syndrome such as von Hippel-Lindau disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history suggesting a hereditary renal cancer syndrome

key_questions.question: Do you work with industrial chemicals, solvents or metals?
key_questions.looking_for: Occupational exposure to trichloroethylene or cadmium

key_questions.question: Have you had any burning with urination, urinary frequency or urgency?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; their presence points to a urinary tract infection rather than a tumor

key_questions.question: Have you had any blood clots in your urine, or passed gravel or stones?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; stones cause colicky pain and gravel, not painless hematuria

accepted_names: Clear cell carcinoma of the kidney
reasoning_points: Painless gross or microscopic hematuria in an older adult, or an incidental solid renal mass on imaging done for another reason
Risk factors such as cigarette smoking, obesity, hypertension, long-term dialysis or a family history of kidney cancer
Dull constant flank or back pain rather than the colicky pain of stones, and absence of dysuria or frequency
Constitutional or paraneoplastic features such as weight loss, fatigue, fever, new hypertension, hypercalcemia or anemia
A palpable flank or abdominal mass or costovertebral angle tenderness on examination
A solid, contrast-enhancing renal cortical mass on multiphasic CT, with possible renal vein or inferior vena cava thrombus or regional lymphadenopathy
Hematuria on urinalysis without dysmorphic red cells or casts, which would instead suggest glomerular disease
Exclusion of look-alikes such as upper tract urothelial carcinoma, renal abscess, polycystic kidney disease, oncocytoma, angiomyolipoma and renal lymphoma
Staging with chest imaging once the diagnosis is confirmed, since stage is the strongest prognostic factor

easy: Older adult with a long smoking history
Painless gross hematuria plus a palpable flank mass
Solid enhancing renal cortical mass on CT
medium: Tumor found incidentally on imaging done for an unrelated complaint, with no urinary symptoms
Microscopic hematuria only, with a normal examination
Paraneoplastic presentation such as new hypertension, hypercalcemia or fever of unknown origin
Cystic or complex renal mass that is harder to characterize on ultrasound
hard: Younger patient with a hereditary syndrome such as von Hippel-Lindau disease and multifocal or bilateral tumors
Patient on dialysis with acquired cystic kidney disease, where symptoms are attributed to uremia
Renal mass with inferior vena cava tumor thrombus presenting as leg edema or abdominal distention
Metastatic disease presenting with bone pain, pathologic fracture or neurologic symptoms before the kidney primary is known
Fat-poor angiomyolipoma or oncocytoma mimicking renal cell carcinoma on imaging
